prompt: What does /64 describe in an IPv6 address?
options: The first 64 bits identify the prefix.
The final 64 bits identify the prefix.
The address contains a total of 64 bits.
explanation: A prefix length counts the leading bits that identify the network. The remaining 128 minus that length are host bits.

whyWrong.1: The prefix is the leading bits, not the final bits.
whyWrong.2: A prefix length is a bit count, not an address count.
whyWrong.3: Every IPv6 address is 128 bits long.

prompt: What is true of fd12:3456:789a:1::a1/64?
options: It is multicast because it begins with f.
It is a unique local address for routed private connectivity.
It is link-local and can never cross a router.
It is global unicast intended for normal public Internet allocation.
explanation: fd falls inside fc00::/7, the unique local range. ULA is routable inside a private network but not on the Internet.

whyWrong.0: Multicast begins ff, not fd.
whyWrong.2: Link-local addresses are in fe80::/10.
whyWrong.3: Global unicast is 2000::/3; fd is not in that range.

prompt: Which TWO groups identify all IPv6 nodes and all IPv6 routers, respectively, on the local link?
explanation: ff02::1 is all nodes and ff02::2 is all routers, both with link-local scope.

whyWrong.2: ff05::2 is all routers with site scope, not link scope.
whyWrong.3: ff02::1:ff00:1 is a solicited-node group, not all nodes.

prompt: One unicast-format address is assigned to servers in several locations, and routing delivers each packet to the nearest one. What is this?
options: Multicast, requiring the address to start ff
Anycast; selection follows the routing system's preferred path
A duplicate that is forbidden even across separate routed links
explanation: Anycast assigns one address to several devices, and routing delivers to the nearest. It has no address range of its own.

whyWrong.0: IPv6 has no broadcast.
whyWrong.1: Multicast delivers to every group member and uses ff00::/8 addresses.
whyWrong.3: Anycast deliberately reuses an address in several places; it is not a conflict.

prompt: A host built its IPv6 address automatically, but its interface ID has no ff:fe. What does that mean?
options: IPv6 cannot operate without a modified EUI-64 identifier.
Another valid identifier method may be in use.
The host must have obtained its address from stateful DHCPv6.
The absence of ff:fe proves Duplicate Address Detection failed.
explanation: Modified EUI-64 is one way to build an interface ID. Hosts often use a random ID with SLAAC instead.

whyWrong.0: IPv6 works with any valid interface ID.
whyWrong.2: SLAAC can use any interface ID, so the suffix does not show DHCPv6 was used.
whyWrong.3: DAD checks uniqueness and does not depend on the ID format.

prompt: A host gets its address and DNS server from stateful DHCPv6. What supplies its default router?
options: A Router Advertisement with a usable nonzero router lifetime
The DHCPv6 address lease always includes the default-router option.
The host uses its DHCPv6-provided DNS server as the router.
The prefix L flag identifies the router by itself.
explanation: The default router comes from the Router Advertisement, not from DHCPv6. DHCPv6 has no default-gateway option.

whyWrong.1: DHCPv6 has no default-router option.
whyWrong.2: A DNS server resolves names; it is not a router.
whyWrong.3: The L flag marks a prefix as on-link and does not name a router.

prompt: Which TWO Neighbor Discovery statements are correct?
options: Address-resolution NS messages can target a solicited-node multicast group.
Every NS is broadcast to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff.
A unicast NS can be used to verify a known neighbor's reachability.
Every stale neighbor entry proves a failed device.
explanation: Address resolution sends NS to a solicited-node multicast group. A unicast NS checks that a known neighbor is still reachable.

whyWrong.1: IPv6 has no broadcast; NS goes to multicast or unicast.
whyWrong.3: A stale entry means reachability is unconfirmed, not that the neighbor failed.

prompt: Which interface command enables IPv6 and creates a link-local address without a global address?
explanation: ipv6 enable turns on IPv6 on the interface and generates a link-local address. It adds no global prefix.

whyWrong.0: This enables IPv6 routing globally and adds no interface address.
whyWrong.2: This configures a global address.
whyWrong.3: This configures IPv4.

prompt: Which is the canonical spelling of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:000a?
explanation: Compress the first of two equal zero runs and drop leading zeros in each group. Use :: only once.

whyWrong.0: Two :: make the address ambiguous.
whyWrong.1: This is valid, but it compresses the second zero run instead of the first.
whyWrong.2: This changes the 1 group to 10.

prompt: Which is the canonical representation of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0a00:0000:0001?
explanation: Drop leading zeros and compress the longest zero run (three groups) with ::. The trailing zeros in a00 are part of the value.

whyWrong.1: Dropping the zeros in a00 changes it to a.
whyWrong.2: Two :: are invalid.
whyWrong.3: This is valid but does not compress the longest zero run.

prompt: An example allocation is 2001:db8:5c00::/56. How many /64s fit, and which is the last?
explanation: 64 minus 56 leaves 8 subnet bits, so 2^8 = 256 /64s. They run from 00 to ff in the last byte of the fourth group.

whyWrong.0: 16 subnets needs only 4 subnet bits.
whyWrong.1: This changes the third group, which the /56 fixes.
whyWrong.3: 65,536 needs 16 subnet bits, but a /56 leaves 8.

prompt: A site has 2001:db8:1200:3400::/56. Which proposed /64 is outside that allocation?
explanation: A /56 fixes the first byte of the fourth group (34), so its /64s run from 3400 to 34ff. 3500 is outside that range.

whyWrong.0: 34ff is the last /64 in the allocation.
whyWrong.1: 34ab starts with 34, so it is inside.
whyWrong.3: 3400 is the first /64 in the allocation.

prompt: What is the prefix containing 2001:db8:5:c7f2::1/60?
explanation: A /60 keeps the first three groups and the first three hex digits of the fourth. Set the last digit to 0.

whyWrong.1: c700 changes retained bits.
whyWrong.2: The last digit lies outside the /60 and must be zero in the prefix.
whyWrong.3: This drops the retained c7f digits.

prompt: What /61 prefix contains 2001:db8:7:ab3d::25/61?
explanation: A /61 keeps the first bit of the last hex digit. d is 1101, so keep the leading 1 and clear the rest to get 1000 (8), covering ab38 to ab3f.

whyWrong.0: This leaves host bits set.
whyWrong.1: ab3c sets a bit that a /61 clears.
whyWrong.2: ab30 clears the retained bit and covers only ab30 to ab37.

prompt: A site needs 20 /64 LANs. What is the smallest block from this list that holds them?
explanation: 5 subnet bits give 2^5 = 32 /64s, and 4 bits give only 16. A /59 is the smallest block that holds 20.

whyWrong.0: A /61 gives 8, fewer than 20.
whyWrong.1: A /64 is a single LAN.
whyWrong.2: A /60 gives 16, fewer than 20.

prompt: MAC 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e uses modified EUI-64 on 2001:db8:10:1::/64. Which address results?
explanation: Insert ff:fe in the middle of the MAC and flip the U/L bit of the first byte, so 00 becomes 02. The identifier is 021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e.

whyWrong.0: The U/L bit was not flipped.
whyWrong.1: ff:fe was inserted in the wrong place.
whyWrong.3: EUI-64 derives the ID from the MAC, not ::1.

prompt: Derive the modified EUI-64 identifier from MAC 02:aa:bb:cc:dd:ee.
explanation: Flip the U/L bit: 02 XOR 02 is 00. Insert ff:fe after the third byte.

whyWrong.0: The U/L bit is flipped, not incremented.
whyWrong.1: ff:fe goes after the first three bytes, not the fourth.
whyWrong.2: The U/L bit was not flipped.

prompt: Which solicited-node multicast group corresponds to 2001:db8:4::ab12:3456?
explanation: Take the last 24 bits (12:3456) and append them to ff02::1:ff00:0/104.

whyWrong.0: The 24 bits must follow the ff02::1:ff prefix.
whyWrong.2: This drops the 12 byte.
whyWrong.3: These are not the last 24 bits.

prompt: R1 uses FE80::1 on Gi0/0 and on Gi0/1, which connect to separate LANs. Which TWO statements are correct?
options: A diagnostic targeting FE80::1 must identify the intended link.
DAD on Gi0/0 checks for the duplicate on Gi0/1.
R1 must forward packets addressed to FE80::1 between those LANs.
The two identical address texts can be valid because the links differ.
A link-local address must be globally unique across the whole enterprise.
explanation: A link-local address only has to be unique on its own link. Identical addresses on separate links are valid, so you must name the interface when you use one.

whyWrong.1: DAD checks only the link it runs on.
whyWrong.2: Routers never forward packets sent to a link-local address.
whyWrong.4: Link-local uniqueness is required per link, not network-wide.

prompt: Which interface command builds the address in 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 using EUI-64?
explanation: The eui-64 keyword makes IOS build the 64-bit interface ID from the interface MAC address.

whyWrong.0: This sets the ID to ::1 by hand.
whyWrong.2: This sets a link-local address.
whyWrong.3: This enables IPv6 and a link-local address but no global address.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
RA source: fe80::1; Router Lifetime: 1800 seconds
Header: M=0, O=1
Prefix: 2001:db8:acad:1::/64; A=1, L=1
No RA DNS option. A working stateless DHCPv6 server supplies DNS.

prompt: A client uses SLAAC plus stateless DHCPv6 with no manual settings. What does it get from each source?
options: DHCPv6 must provide the default router.
A=1 forces the host to derive its identifier from its MAC.
The host cannot form an address without M=1.
SLAAC address, DHCPv6 DNS, and RA-learned default router.
explanation: The RA with A=1 gives the prefix for SLAAC. O=1 tells the host to ask DHCPv6 for DNS, and the default router comes from the RA.

whyWrong.0: The default router comes from the RA, not DHCPv6.
whyWrong.1: SLAAC can use any interface ID, not only EUI-64.
whyWrong.2: SLAAC does not need M=1; M asks for a DHCPv6 address.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
Complete relevant R1 settings:
no ipv6 unicast-routing
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
 no shutdown
Interface up/up; no other advertising router exists.

prompt: Automatic PCs get only link-local addresses, yet R1 answers a manually addressed PC. What is missing on R1?
options: IPv6 forwarding/router operation has not been enabled globally.
IPv6 processing has not been enabled on the addressed interface.
The manual global address must first be replaced by an EUI-64 address.
The RA managed-address flag must be set for all SLAAC clients.
explanation: Without ipv6 unicast-routing, R1 does not send RAs or forward IPv6 packets.

whyWrong.1: R1 already answers the PC, so IPv6 is enabled on the interface.
whyWrong.2: The manual address is valid, and EUI-64 does not enable routing.
whyWrong.3: SLAAC does not need the M flag.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
PC-A: 2001:db8:acad:1::10/64
PC-A gateway: 2001:db8:acad:10::1
R1 Gi0/0 up/up:
 FE80::1
 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1
No router owns 2001:db8:acad:10::1.

prompt: PC-A cannot reach its manually configured gateway. What is wrong?
options: The PC must obtain its gateway from DHCPv6 instead of using the documented manual address.
The PC should widen its prefix to /48 while retaining the gateway text.
The PC cannot use a manually configured global-form gateway.
The PC names acad:10::1, but the actual router address is acad:1::1.
explanation: The PC points to acad:10::1, but R1 has acad:1::1. The gateway must match an address on the router.

whyWrong.0: DHCPv6 does not supply a default router.
whyWrong.1: A shorter prefix cannot fix a wrong gateway address.
whyWrong.2: A manual global gateway is valid.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
Complete Gi0/1 address configuration:
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64
 ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
Displayed addresses:
 FE80::1
 2001:DB8:ACAD:2:21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E

prompt: Hosts use 2001:db8:acad:2::1 as their gateway. What does the R1 output show?
options: The eui-64 keyword guarantees ::1 also exists.
The manual link-local address also creates a global address with the same ::1 suffix.
Clearing the PC neighbor cache will create the missing ::1 address on R1.
The derived address exists, but the expected ::1 is absent.
explanation: R1 has the EUI-64 address but not ::1. A gateway must match an address configured on the router.

whyWrong.0: eui-64 builds one derived address, not ::1.
whyWrong.1: A manual link-local address does not create a global address.
whyWrong.2: Clearing the cache cannot add an address to R1.

prompt: A host reports a duplicate address. What do you do?
options: Clear the router neighbor cache and assume the address is unique.
Investigate which device on this link already uses that address before assigning it.
Change the address from uppercase to lowercase.
Disable DAD so both hosts can use the planned address.
explanation: DAD reports another device on the link using the address. Find that device and assign unique addresses.

whyWrong.0: Clearing the cache does not remove the other device.
whyWrong.2: Letter case does not change the address.
whyWrong.3: Disabling DAD hides the conflict but leaves it.

prompt: What is the smallest repair that fits the addressing plan?
options: Change PC-B gateway to R1 LAN 1 global address.
Change both router LANs to /48 to make the mistaken host prefix fit.
Change PC-B to 2001:db8:26:2::20/64 and keep its link-local gateway.
Replace the gateway with ::1 because it always means the local router.
explanation: PC-B is on LAN 2 but has a LAN 1 prefix. Give it an address in the LAN 2 /64 and keep its gateway.

whyWrong.0: The LAN 1 router address is not on PC-B link.
whyWrong.1: A /48 on both LANs overlaps them and breaks the /64 plan.
whyWrong.3: ::1 is not a gateway address.

exhibit.title: Approved and configured LAN prefixes (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Plan: LAN 1 = 2001:db8:26:1::/64; LAN 2 = 2001:db8:26:2::/64
R1 LAN 2: 2001:db8:26:2::1/64, FE80::1, up/up
PC-B on LAN 2: 2001:db8:26:1::20/64, gateway FE80::1
PC-B reaches FE80::1 locally; remote hosts have the intended two LAN prefixes.

prompt: Which TWO conclusions does the exhibit support?
options: A static route to either directly connected /64 is the missing prerequisite.
Successful local ping proves that R1 forwards between the LANs.
The LAN 1 host can resolve and reach its router as an endpoint.
The failure proves that the LAN 2 host has a duplicate IPv6 address.
IPv6 forwarding is missing even though both connected interfaces have addresses.
explanation: Each PC reaches R1 itself, so the interfaces work. The PCs cannot reach each other because ipv6 unicast-routing is missing, so R1 does not forward.

whyWrong.0: The prefixes are connected, so no static route is needed.
whyWrong.1: Reaching R1 itself does not show R1 forwards between LANs.
whyWrong.3: The exhibit shows no duplicate address.

exhibit.title: Local replies without transit forwarding (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1 Gi0/0: 2001:db8:28:1::1/64 up/up
R1 Gi0/1: 2001:db8:28:2::1/64 up/up
Global: no ipv6 unicast-routing; no filters
PCs have the matching /64 and their own on-link R1 gateway.
Each PC can ping its own R1 interface; PC-to-PC ping fails.

prompt: How many bits does one hexadecimal digit represent?
explanation: One hexadecimal digit represents 4 bits, so a 4-digit group is 16 bits.

whyWrong.0: 2 bits would be a base-4 digit.
whyWrong.2: 8 bits is two hex digits.
whyWrong.3: 16 bits is a full four-digit group.

prompt: Which protocol carries IPv6 Neighbor Discovery messages?
explanation: Neighbor Discovery runs over ICMPv6 and replaces ARP in IPv6.

whyWrong.0: ARP is IPv4 only.
whyWrong.2: DHCPv6 assigns configuration; it does not carry ND.
whyWrong.3: IGMP manages IPv4 multicast groups.

prompt: What prefix length does an ordinary Ethernet LAN using SLAAC use?
explanation: SLAAC LANs use a /64, leaving 64 bits for the interface ID.

whyWrong.0: A /48 is a typical site allocation, not a LAN prefix.
whyWrong.1: A /56 is a typical allocation to a small site.
whyWrong.3: A /128 identifies a single host address.

prompt: Which IPv6 address is the loopback address?
explanation: ::1 is the IPv6 loopback address.

whyWrong.0: :: is the unspecified address.
whyWrong.2: fe80::1 is a link-local address.
whyWrong.3: ff02::1 is the all-nodes multicast group.
